title: Group Anagrams
description: Group a list of words so that words that are anagrams of each other end up together.
statement:
Given a list of lowercase `words`, group together the words that are anagrams of each other, and return the groups as a list of lists.

- Every word goes into exactly one group, and all the words of a group are anagrams of each other.
- Repeated words are all kept: `["a", "a"]` gives `[["a", "a"]]`.
- The order of the groups, and the order of the words inside a group, do not matter (the tests sort both before comparing).
- The empty string is a word like any other (`[""]` gives `[[""]]`). An empty list gives `[]`.

**Examples**

```python
group_anagrams(["eat", "tea", "tan", "ate", "nat", "bat"])
# [["eat", "tea", "ate"], ["tan", "nat"], ["bat"]]   in any order
group_anagrams([""])      # [[""]]
group_anagrams(["a"])     # [["a"]]
```

Comparing every word with every other word is too slow for the last test (about 17,000 words).
tests:
rng = random.Random(3)
many_words, many_groups = [], []
for letters in itertools.combinations_with_replacement("abcdefghijklmn", 5):
    shuffled = list(letters)
    rng.shuffle(shuffled)
    group = ["".join(letters), "".join(shuffled)]
    many_words += group
    many_groups.append(sorted(group))
rng.shuffle(many_words)
assert as_groups(group_anagrams(many_words)) == sorted(many_groups), "too slow or wrong on about 17,000 words"
hints: Two words are anagrams exactly when they have the same letters. Can you give every word a "fingerprint" that is identical for all of its anagrams?
Sorting the letters of a word gives such a fingerprint. Use it as a dictionary key whose value is the list of words with that fingerprint.
A list cannot be a dictionary key, but a string or a tuple can. And comparing every word with every other word will time out on the last test.
explanation:
**The idea.** All the anagrams of a word have the same letters, so sorting the letters of a word gives a "fingerprint" that every anagram shares: `"eat"`, `"tea"` and `"ate"` all become `"aet"`. Use the fingerprint as a dictionary key and collect the words that share it.

**Why a string key.** Dictionary keys must be hashable. A list of letters is not, but `"".join(sorted(word))` is a string, and a tuple of letter counts would be too.

**Complexity.** For n words of length up to k, O(n · k log k) time. Counting the letters into a tuple of 26 numbers instead of sorting makes the key O(k), so the whole thing O(n · k) for lowercase words. Comparing every word with every other word would be O(n²).

**Follow-up.** How would you handle capital letters or accents? Decide whether `"Eat"` and `"tea"` are anagrams, then lowercase or normalise each word before you build its key.
